w001.tone_note_en: Dictionary tone 3. In 你好, nǐ is usually pronounced like ní before hǎo.

w002.tone_note_en: Tone 3; before shì, wǒ usually stays low without a full rise.

w003.tone_note_en: Tone 1: high and level. It sounds the same as 她.

w004.tone_note_en: Tone 1, with the same pronunciation as 他; the written character indicates the person referred to.

w005.tone_note_en: Wǒ has tone 3; men is neutral. Whether we includes the listener depends on context; Mandarin uses the same word for both.

w006.tone_note_en: Dictionary tone 3. In the greeting 你好, nǐ changes while hǎo keeps tone 3.

w007.tone_note_en: Tone 4: falling. 是 links a person or thing to an identity; it is not used in every sentence describing a quality.

w008.tone_note_en: Dictionary tone 4. Before shì, which has tone 4, it is usually pronounced bú.

w009.tone_note_en: Xiè has tone 4; the second xie is usually neutral.

w010.tone_note_en: Tones 4 + 4; the first falling tone is usually shorter.

w011.tone_note_en: Dictionary tone 1: yí before tone 4, yì before tones 1, 2 or 3. Keep yī when counting or in 第一.

w012.tone_note_en: Tone 4. 二 is used when counting; 两 is used in many quantity patterns taught later.

w014.tone_note_en: Tone 4. Listen to s at the front of the mouth, unlike sh in 是.

w015.tone_note_en: Tone 3; before gè it usually stays low without a full rise.

w016.tone_note_en: Tone 4; iu is the shortened spelling of the final iou.

w017.tone_note_en: Tone 1. Q has a clear puff of air.

w018.tone_note_en: Tone 1. B has less of a puff of air than p.

w019.tone_note_en: Tone 3; before gè it usually stays low. Iu is one final, not two syllables.

w020.tone_note_en: Tone 2: rising. For sh, the tongue tip is slightly farther back.

w022.tone_note_en: Mā has tone 1; the second syllable in 妈妈 is usually neutral: māma. This is the pronunciation of this word, not a rule for all repeated characters.

w023.example_meaning_en: My older brother is a teacher.

w024.example_meaning_en: My older sister is at school.

w025.example_meaning_en: My younger brother is at home.

w027.tone_note_en: Dictionary tones: 2 + neutral. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.

w028.tone_note_en: Nǚ has tone 3; ér has tone 2. The connected pronunciation is nǚ’ér.

w034.example_meaning_en: My paternal grandfather is at home.

w036.example_meaning_en: My maternal grandfather is in Malaysia.

w038.meaning_en: father's younger brother; uncle (form of address)
w038.tone_note_en: Shū has tone 1; the second syllable is neutral. As a family relationship, 叔叔 specifically means the father's younger brother; it is also a form of address for an adult man.

w039.tone_note_en: Ā has tone 1; yí has tone 2. 阿姨 is also a form of address for an adult woman, who need not be a relative.

w043.tone_note_en: Xué has tone 2; 生 in 学生 is usually neutral: xuésheng.

w053.tone_note_en: Cài has tone 4; 菜 can also refer to a prepared dish.

w054.tone_note_en: The dictionary tones of shuǐguǒ are 3 + 3. In connected speech, shuǐ usually rises like shuí before guǒ; the dictionary spelling is retained.

w058.example_meaning_en: The weather is hot; I want to eat watermelon.

w061.tone_note_en: Dictionary tone: 3. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.
w061.example_meaning_en: Please give me a glass of water.

w063.example_meaning_en: Dad drinks coffee in the morning.

w064.example_meaning_en: I want to drink fruit juice.

w065.tone_note_en: Dictionary tone: 2. The example keeps dictionary bù; before tone-4 yào, 不 usually sounds like bú.

w066.example_meaning_en: There is salt in the soup.

w067.example_meaning_en: This dish has a lot of oil.

w069.tone_note_en: Fàn has tone 4. In 吃饭, it means eating or having a meal, not necessarily eating rice alone.

w070.example_meaning_en: I have breakfast at seven o'clock.

w071.example_meaning_en: We have lunch at twelve o'clock.

w080.example_meaning_en: There are onions in the dish.

w082.example_meaning_en: This dish has chilli in it.

w085.example_meaning_en: I want to eat cake on my birthday.

w086.example_meaning_en: The weather is hot; I want to eat ice cream.

w088.example_meaning_en: This dish has peanuts in it.

w089.tone_note_en: The dictionary tones of mǐfěn are 3 + 3; mǐ usually rises like mí before fěn. 米粉 can mean rice noodles (including thin rice vermicelli) or rice flour, depending on context.
w089.example_meaning_en: I eat rice noodles for lunch.

w090.example_meaning_en: We eat fried rice for lunch.

w091.tone_note_en: Shā and lā both have tone 1. 沙拉 is a common loanword.

w092.tone_note_en: Qīng and zhēn have tone 1. 清真 is used for food prepared according to Islamic practice and in compounds such as 清真寺 (mosque); it does not replace every use of the word Islam. The example keeps dictionary yī; before tone-1 jiā, 一 usually sounds like yì.

w093.tone_note_en: Jiā has tone 1; its meaning depends on context.

w094.example_meaning_en: I go to school every day.

w096.example_meaning_en: I go to the shop to buy water.

w097.example_meaning_en: The supermarket is next to the school.

w098.tone_note_en: Fàn and diàn have tone 4. 饭店 can mean a restaurant or a hotel, depending on context.

w100.tone_note_en: Yín has tone 2; 行 in 银行 is pronounced háng, tone 2.
w100.example_meaning_en: The bank is next to the shop.

w102.example_meaning_en: The airport is far from here.

w105.example_meaning_en: The library is next to the school.

w109.example_meaning_en: Dad watches television in the living room.

w110.tone_note_en: Dictionary tones: 4 + 4. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.

w112.tone_note_en: Chuāng has tone 1 and means window. 窗户 chuānghu is another common, two-syllable form; 窗 is not a spelling abbreviation or a traditional character.

w113.example_meaning_en: The book is on the table.

w115.example_meaning_en: The child is sleeping on the bed.

w118.tone_note_en: Dictionary tones: 2 + 4. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.
w118.example_meaning_en: Kuala Lumpur is a big city.

w119.tone_note_en: Dictionary tones: 2 + 1. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.

w123.meaning_ms: metro; kereta api bandar bawah tanah
w123.tone_note_en: Dì has tone 4; tiě has tone 3. 地铁 refers to a metro system, which may also have above-ground sections; it is not the name for every kind of train.
w123.example_meaning_en: We take the metro to school.

w124.example_meaning_en: I take the bus to the shop.

w125.example_meaning_en: We take the train to Kuala Lumpur.

w126.example_meaning_en: The aeroplane is at the airport.

w127.example_meaning_en: I take a taxi to the hospital.

w128.tone_note_en: Dictionary tones: 4 + 1. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.

w129.tone_note_en: Zì has tone 4; 行 in 自行 is pronounced xíng, tone 2; chē has tone 1.

w130.tone_note_en: Mó has tone 2; tuō and chē have tone 1. Do not give all three syllables tone 1.
w130.example_meaning_en: My older brother rides a motorcycle.

w131.example_meaning_en: The boat is on the water.

w135.tone_note_en: Zhè has tone 4; lǐ has tone 3. The pronunciation lǐ is common in Standard Mandarin.

w137.tone_note_en: The dictionary tones of nǎlǐ are 3 + 3. When both syllables carry full tones, nǎ usually rises like ná before lǐ; it is not simply lowered.

w138.example_meaning_en: Today I am going to school.

w139.example_meaning_en: We are going to the park tomorrow.

w142.example_meaning_en: I drink tea in the morning.

w143.example_meaning_en: I am at school in the morning.

w145.example_meaning_en: I go to the shop in the afternoon.

w146.example_meaning_en: I rest at home in the evening.

w147.example_meaning_en: When are you going to school?

w149.example_meaning_en: I have lived in Malaysia for three years.

w150.tone_note_en: Yuè has tone 4; month names use a number before 月.

w151.tone_note_en: Rì has tone 4. For dates, 月 followed by a number and 日 is fairly formal; everyday speech also uses 号 hào.

w152.example_meaning_en: What day of the week is it today?

w154.tone_note_en: Dictionary tones: 3 + 2. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.

w155.tone_note_en: Diǎn has tone 3. For clock time, the hour number comes before 点: 三点 sān diǎn is three o'clock; a number after 点 may indicate minutes.

w156.example_meaning_en: It is half past three now.

w158.example_meaning_en: I go to the park at the weekend.

w166.tone_note_en: Rè has tone 4; tiān has tone 1. 热天 means hot days or a hot season; 天气很热 is also common when describing the current weather.
w166.example_meaning_en: On hot days, you need to drink more water.

w167.example_meaning_en: The weather is pleasantly cool in the evening.

w169.tone_note_en: Kuài has tone 4; it is a spoken unit of money, particularly in China, rather than the name of the Malaysian currency.

w170.tone_note_en: Yuán has tone 2; it is a formal unit of currency, particularly for renminbi.

w171.tone_note_en: Jiǎo has tone 3. This unit is one tenth of a yuan and is not a unit of the ringgit.

w172.meaning_en: fen (one hundredth of a yuan); minute
w172.tone_note_en: Fēn has tone 1. In renminbi, one fen is one hundredth of a yuan; 分 can also mean a minute. The example keeps dictionary yī; both instances of 一 in the example are usually pronounced yì.
w172.example_meaning_en: One yuan equals one hundred fen.

w173.example_meaning_en: What is the price of this apple?

w178.tone_note_en: Mài has tone 4; distinguish it from 买 mǎi (to buy).

w180.example_meaning_en: I do not have any cash.

w181.tone_note_en: Yín and háng have tone 2; kǎ has tone 3.
w181.example_meaning_en: I pay using a bank card.

w183.tone_note_en: Zhǎo has tone 3; qián has tone 2. In a payment context, 找钱 means giving change back, rather than looking for lost money.
w183.example_meaning_en: The shop assistant gives me change.

w185.tone_note_en: Dictionary tones: 2 + 2. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.

w186.example_meaning_en: I go shopping at the weekend.

w187.tone_note_en: Dǎ has tone 3; 折 is zhé, tone 2, when referring to a discount.
w187.example_meaning_en: This shop is offering a discount today.

w188.tone_note_en: Chūn has tone 1; jié has tone 2. This festival name refers to a Chinese tradition.
w188.example_meaning_en: We visit family during Chinese New Year.

w189.example_meaning_en: We eat mooncakes during the Mid-Autumn Festival.

w190.example_meaning_en: We eat zongzi during the Dragon Boat Festival.

w191.example_meaning_en: We eat tangyuan during the Lantern Festival.

w192.tone_note_en: Guó has tone 2; qìng has tone 4; jié has tone 2. The reference here is specifically to China.
w192.example_meaning_en: China's National Day is on 1 October.

w194.tone_note_en: Kāi and zhāi have tone 1; jié has tone 2. 开斋节 is a common Mandarin term for Eid al-Fitr.
w194.example_meaning_en: I visit family during Eid al-Fitr.

w195.tone_note_en: Tú has tone 2; yāo has tone 1; jié has tone 2. 屠妖节 is a common regional Mandarin term for Deepavali in Malaysia and Singapore.

w196.tone_note_en: Xīn has tone 1; nián has tone 2. The reference can be general or to a particular festival.

w197.tone_note_en: Jié has tone 2; rì has tone 4. The example keeps dictionary yī; before tone-4 gè, 一 usually sounds like yí.
w197.example_meaning_en: Chinese New Year is a traditional festival.

w198.tone_note_en: 假 is jià, tone 4, when it means a holiday; qī has tone 1.
w198.example_meaning_en: I rest at home during the holidays.

w199.example_meaning_en: We eat mooncakes during the Mid-Autumn Festival.

w200.example_meaning_en: We eat zongzi during the Dragon Boat Festival.

w201.example_meaning_en: I give the children red envelopes containing money during Chinese New Year.

w202.example_meaning_en: I buy a present for Mum.

w203.meaning_en: good wishes; to wish someone well
w203.example_meaning_en: Thank you for your good wishes.

w204.tone_note_en: Kuài has tone 4; 乐 is lè, tone 4, in 快乐.

w210.meaning_en: to look; to watch; to read
w210.tone_note_en: Kàn has tone 4; its specific meaning depends on the object.
w210.example_meaning_en: I watch television in the evening.

w216.example_meaning_en: My father works in Kuala Lumpur.

w217.example_meaning_en: I rest at home in the evening.

w218.tone_note_en: Shuì has tone 4; 觉 is jiào, tone 4, in 睡觉.
w218.example_meaning_en: The child goes to sleep at nine o'clock at night.

w219.example_meaning_en: I get up at six o'clock in the morning.

w221.example_meaning_en: A friend is coming to my home today.

w222.example_meaning_en: I go home in the evening.

w224.example_meaning_en: He runs in the park every day.

w225.meaning_en: to sit; to take a vehicle
w225.tone_note_en: Zuò has tone 4; with the name of a vehicle, it means taking that vehicle.

w226.tone_note_en: Zhàn has tone 4; as a noun, it can also mean a station.

w227.tone_note_en: Kāi has tone 1; its meaning changes with the object.

w228.tone_note_en: Guān has tone 1; with a device, it can mean turning it off.

w230.example_meaning_en: I use my phone to look at the map.

w231.tone_note_en: Gěi has tone 3; it can also mark the recipient before a verb.

w237.tone_note_en: Huì has tone 4; it often expresses a learned ability or a possibility.

w238.tone_note_en: Néng has tone 2; it often expresses ability or that circumstances make something possible.

w239.tone_note_en: The dictionary tones of kěyǐ are 3 + 3. In connected speech, kě usually rises like ké before yǐ; it is not simply lowered.

w240.tone_note_en: Yào has tone 4; it can express a wish or a need. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.
w240.example_meaning_en: I want a cup of tea.

w241.tone_note_en: Dictionary tone: 3. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.

w242.meaning_ms: tiada; tidak mempunyai; belum (dengan kata kerja)
w242.meaning_en: not have; there is no; not yet (before a verb)

w243.meaning_en: to be at; at; in progress
w243.tone_note_en: Zài has tone 4; before a verb, 在 can also mark an action in progress.

w245.tone_note_en: Jiào has tone 4; the name in the sentence is an example name.

w246.example_meaning_en: I want to ask the teacher.

w251.tone_note_en: 少 is shǎo, tone 3, when it means few or little; it is shào, tone 4, when it means young.
w251.example_meaning_en: There is little water in the glass.

w252.tone_note_en: 长 is cháng, tone 2, when it means long; the same character is zhǎng when it means a leader or growing.

w255.tone_note_en: Ǎi has tone 3; when used for a person, it refers to their height.
w255.example_meaning_en: He is neither tall nor short.

w257.tone_note_en: Màn has tone 4. The example keeps dictionary yī; before tone 3 in this example, 一 usually sounds like yì.
w257.example_meaning_en: Please speak a little more slowly.

w259.tone_note_en: Jiù has tone 4; it refers to something old or previously used.

w263.tone_note_en: Lèi has tone 4; other meanings and tones occur in the readings léi and lěi.

w264.tone_note_en: Duì has tone 4; in this sentence, it means correct.

w267.tone_note_en: Nán has tone 2 when it means difficult; the character has other readings in particular contexts.

w268.example_meaning_en: What do you want to eat?

w269.tone_note_en: 谁 is commonly pronounced shéi (tone 2); shuí also exists as a variant.

w272.tone_note_en: Jǐ has tone 3; it is usually used for a fairly small number or in questions about time.
w272.example_meaning_en: How many friends do you have?

w273.tone_note_en: Nǎ has tone 3. 哪个 nǎge means which; the spoken variant něige also exists. Keep nǎ for this practice.
w273.example_meaning_en: Which city do you live in?

w274.tone_note_en: Zhè has tone 4; before a classifier it is often pronounced as in zhège.

w275.tone_note_en: Nà has tone 4; before a classifier it is often pronounced as in nàge.

w276.tone_note_en: De is usually neutral and links a possessor or description to a noun.

w277.meaning_en: particle marking completion or a new situation
w277.tone_note_en: Le is usually neutral. It can show that something has happened or mark a new situation; it is not a past-tense marker for every sentence. In the example, the speaker says they have eaten.

w279.example_meaning_en: My notebook is on the table.

w282.example_meaning_en: I use a computer to study.

w283.example_meaning_en: We watch television in the evening.

w285.example_meaning_en: My shoes are beside the door.

w288.example_meaning_en: The sun is strong; please wear a hat.

w289.example_meaning_en: My bag is on the chair.

w290.tone_note_en: The dictionary tones of yǔsǎn are 3 + 3. In connected speech, yǔ usually rises like yú before sǎn; it is not simply lowered.
w290.example_meaning_en: It is raining; I am taking an umbrella.

w291.example_meaning_en: My glasses are on the table.

w292.tone_note_en: Dictionary tones: 1 + neutral. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.
w292.example_meaning_en: There is a cup on the table.

w293.tone_note_en: Dictionary tone: 3. The example keeps dictionary yī; in this quantity pattern, 一 usually sounds like yí before tone 4 and yì before tones 1, 2 or 3.

w294.example_meaning_en: The plate is on the table.

w296.tone_note_en: Sháo has tone 2; zi is usually neutral. The example keeps dictionary yī; before tone 3 in this example, 一 usually sounds like yì.
w296.example_meaning_en: There is a spoon in the bowl.

w297.tone_note_en: Tóu has tone 2 when it means head; the suffix 头 in some other words can be neutral.

u0-initials-1-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial b: Close and release the lips. Use less of a puff of air than for p; do not add a vowel after the letter b.
u0-initials-1-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-1-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial p: Close and release the lips with a clear puff of air. Compare it with b in bā.
u0-initials-1-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-1-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial m: Keep the lips together and let the voice pass through the nose, then open into a.
u0-initials-1-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-2-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial f: Let the upper teeth touch the lower lip lightly while air flows out.
u0-initials-2-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-2-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial d: Touch the tongue tip just behind the upper teeth; use little puff of air.
u0-initials-2-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-2-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial t: Place the tongue much as for d, but release a stronger puff of air.
u0-initials-2-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-3-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial n: Place the tongue tip behind the upper teeth; let the voice pass through the nose.
u0-initials-3-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-3-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial l: Place the tongue tip behind the upper teeth; air flows around the sides of the tongue. Distinguish it from n.
u0-initials-3-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-3-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial g: Touch the back of the tongue to the soft palate; use little puff of air.
u0-initials-3-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-4-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial k: Place the tongue as for g, but release a clear puff of air.
u0-initials-4-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-4-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial h: Let air create friction at the back of the mouth; listen to hē.
u0-initials-4-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-4-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial j: Position the tongue towards the front of the hard palate, without rounding the lips. Use little puff of air.
u0-initials-4-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-5-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial q: Place the tongue as for j, with a clear puff of air. The spelling q does not represent a k sound.
u0-initials-5-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-5-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial x: Let air create friction between the tongue and the front of the palate; do not read it as the letter x in Malay.
u0-initials-5-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-5-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial zh: Raise the tongue tip slightly back. Use little puff of air; compare it with z later.
u0-initials-5-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-6-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial ch: Place the tongue tip as for zh, with a clear puff of air.
u0-initials-6-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-6-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial sh: Keep the tongue tip slightly back while air creates continuous friction.
u0-initials-6-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-6-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial r: Keep the tongue tip slightly back. Listen for gentle friction; do not roll r as in some Malay pronunciations.
u0-initials-6-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-7-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial z: Keep the tongue tip near the back of the upper teeth; use little puff of air. The tongue is farther forward than for zh.
u0-initials-7-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-7-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial c: Place the tongue as for z, with a clear puff of air. It is not the c sound in the Malay word cara.
u0-initials-7-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-initials-7-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Initial s: Let air create friction near the back of the upper teeth. Distinguish s from sh, where the tongue is farther back.
u0-initials-7-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-1-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Final a: Open the mouth comfortably. Listen to a in bā.
u0-finals-1-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-1-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Final o: Round the lips. Listen to o after b in bō.
u0-finals-1-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-1-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Final e: Keep the tongue towards the back and the lips unrounded. This sound is not the same as e in every Malay word.
u0-finals-1-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-2-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Final i, as in yī: Spread the lips slightly. Y helps spell a syllable with no initial consonant.
u0-finals-2-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-2-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Final u, as in wū: Round the lips and keep the tongue towards the back. W helps spell a syllable with no initial consonant.
u0-finals-2-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-2-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Final ü: Position the tongue as for i, but round the lips. In yú, the dots over ü are omitted in writing; the sound remains ü.
u0-finals-2-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-3-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ai moves from a towards i within one syllable.
u0-finals-3-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-3-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ei moves from e towards i; listen to běi.
u0-finals-3-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-3-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ao moves from a towards an o sound; keep it within one syllable.
u0-finals-3-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-3-4.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ou moves from o towards u within one syllable.
u0-finals-3-4.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-4-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ia: Let i glide directly into a in jiā; these are not two syllables.
u0-finals-4-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-4-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ie: Let i glide towards an e that is more open than the e in gē.
u0-finals-4-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-4-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ua: Move from rounded lips towards a in huā.
u0-finals-4-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-4-4.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Uo: Listen to the glide from u towards o in duō.
u0-finals-4-4.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-4-5.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Üe: Begin with rounded lips as for ü. In yuè, the dots over ü are omitted, as in jué, què and xué.
u0-finals-4-5.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-5-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. An ends with the tongue tip touching behind the upper teeth. Do not add a vowel after n.
u0-finals-5-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-5-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. En also ends with n; distinguish its vowel from an.
u0-finals-5-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-5-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ang ends at the back of the tongue, with ng; the tongue tip does not close against the upper teeth.
u0-finals-5-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-5-4.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Eng ends with ng; compare the tongue position with en.
u0-finals-5-4.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-5-5.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ong has rounded lips and ends with ng at the back of the tongue.
u0-finals-5-5.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-6-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Iao: Listen to xiǎo as one syllable with a continuous glide.
u0-finals-6-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-6-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Iou is written iu after an initial: liù. The tone mark is placed on u.
u0-finals-6-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-6-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Uai: Let u glide into ai within the single syllable kuài.
u0-finals-6-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-6-4.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Uei is written ui after an initial: shuǐ. The tone mark is placed on i.
u0-finals-6-4.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-6-5.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Uan: Let u glide into an, ending with n at the front of the mouth.
u0-finals-6-5.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-7-1.meaning_ms: 先: dahulu; 元: yuan (unit wang)
u0-finals-7-1.meaning_en: 先: first; 元: yuan (unit of money)
u0-finals-7-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ian and üan: Compare xiān with yuán. Begin üan with rounded lips; the spelling yuan omits the dots over ü.
u0-finals-7-1.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-7-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. In and ün: Compare xīn with yún. In yun, the dots over ü are not written, but the sound remains ü.
u0-finals-7-2.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-7-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Iang and uang: Compare the initial i glide in xiāng with the rounded u in guāng. Both end with ng.
u0-finals-7-3.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-7-4.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ing and iong: Listen to xīng and xiōng; the lips are more rounded in iong. Both end with ng.
u0-finals-7-4.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-finals-7-5.meaning_ms: 轮: roda; 翁: lelaki tua
u0-finals-7-5.meaning_en: 轮: wheel; 翁: elderly man
u0-finals-7-5.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Uen is written un after an initial: lún ends with n. Ueng appears as weng without an initial consonant: wēng ends with ng. Compare them carefully.
u0-finals-7-5.tone_note_en: The tone marks in pinyin show dictionary tones. Focus on the sound first; do not guess its pronunciation from Malay spelling.

u0-tones-1-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Tone 1: Keep the voice high and level, like a horizontal line.
u0-tones-1-1.tone_note_en: Mā means mother; the straight mark indicates tone 1.

u0-tones-1-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Tone 2: Raise the voice from mid to high. Compare it with mā.
u0-tones-1-2.tone_note_en: Má means hemp or flax; this example is only for listening to the tone.

u0-tones-1-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Tone 3 in isolation: Let the voice fall low, then it may rise. In connected speech, the rising part is often incomplete.
u0-tones-1-3.tone_note_en: Mǎ means horse. Do not force a full dip-and-rise contour onto every tone 3 in a sentence.

u0-tones-2-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Tone 4: Let the voice fall firmly from high to low.
u0-tones-2-1.tone_note_en: Mà means to scold; listen to it only as a tone comparison.

u0-tones-2-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. The second ma has a neutral tone: it is short and unstressed. Its pitch depends on the preceding syllable.
u0-tones-2-2.tone_note_en: In māma, the second ma is neutral, not tone-1 mā. This is the pronunciation of the word, not a rule that every repeated character becomes neutral.

u0-tones-2-3.meaning_ms: partikel di hujung soalan ya atau tidak
u0-tones-2-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Ma at the end of a question is usually neutral. Listen to the short syllable without lengthening it.
u0-tones-2-3.tone_note_en: The absence of a tone mark on ma indicates a neutral tone; 0 is a practice label, not a fixed fifth tone.

u0-tone-pairs-1-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Follow a high, level tone with a rising tone: tones 1 + 2. This means China.
u0-tone-pairs-1-1.tone_note_en: Zhōngguó retains both dictionary tones; do not give the whole word a single tone.

u0-tone-pairs-1-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Listen to rising xué followed by neutral sheng. This means student.
u0-tone-pairs-1-2.tone_note_en: In the usual pronunciation xuésheng, sheng is neutral; its pitch depends on context.

u0-tone-pairs-1-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Two tone-4 syllables: Listen for two falls, with the first often shorter. This means goodbye.
u0-tone-pairs-1-3.tone_note_en: Dictionary tones 4 + 4; the exact pitch contours vary with speaking speed and speaker.

u0-tone-pairs-2-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. The dictionary tones are 3 + 3. In the ordinary greeting, nǐ changes to a rising tone like ní before hǎo.
u0-tone-pairs-2-1.tone_note_en: Dictionary pinyin: nǐ hǎo; usual pronunciation: ní hǎo. This sound change does not change the meaning or the writing.

u0-tone-pairs-2-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Dictionary tones 3 + 3: hěn is usually pronounced like hén before hǎo. This means very good.
u0-tone-pairs-2-2.tone_note_en: Dictionary pinyin: hěn hǎo; usual connected pronunciation: hén hǎo. Longer sequences depend on how words are grouped.

u0-tone-pairs-2-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Tone 3 followed by tone 1: lǎo usually stays low without a full rise, then shī is high and level. This means teacher.
u0-tone-pairs-2-3.tone_note_en: Dictionary tones 3 + 1. A low tone 3 before another tone is not the same as changing to tone 2.

u0-sandhi-bu-1.meaning_en: is not; am not; are not
u0-sandhi-bu-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. The dictionary tones of bù shì are 4 + 4; before tone 4, 不 is usually pronounced bú. This means is not.
u0-sandhi-bu-1.tone_note_en: Dictionary pinyin: bù shì; connected pronunciation: bú shì.

u0-sandhi-bu-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Before tone 3, 不 keeps bù. This means not good.
u0-sandhi-bu-2.tone_note_en: The change from bù to bú occurs before tone 4, not before every tone.

u0-sandhi-bu-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. When said alone or with emphasis, listen to the dictionary form bù.
u0-sandhi-bu-3.tone_note_en: In an A不A pattern such as 是不是, 不 can become neutral. That is another pattern to learn later; do not apply the bú rule blindly.

u0-sandhi-yi-1.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. When counting or saying this number alone, 一 is pronounced yī: one.
u0-sandhi-yi-1.tone_note_en: The dictionary tone is 1. In serial numbers or after 第 in an ordinal number, yī is usually retained.

u0-sandhi-yi-2.meaning_en: one item; one person (depending on context)
u0-sandhi-yi-2.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Before tone 4, 一 is usually pronounced yí. It means one item or one person, depending on what is being referred to.
u0-sandhi-yi-2.tone_note_en: Dictionary pinyin: yī gè; basic connected pronunciation: yí gè. 个 also often becomes neutral in speech.

u0-sandhi-yi-3.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. Before tones 1, 2 or 3, 一 is usually pronounced yì. This example means one day.
u0-sandhi-yi-3.tone_note_en: Dictionary pinyin: yī tiān; connected pronunciation: yì tiān.

u0-sandhi-yi-4.explanation_en: Listen first, replay the audio slowly, then try saying it. In the ordinal number 第一, 一 keeps yī. This means first.
u0-sandhi-yi-4.tone_note_en: Distinguish ordinal numbers from quantities. In a verb–一–verb pattern, 一 can become neutral; learn that pattern later.
